newsitem.title: FRANCE: French markets defensive as election looms.
newsitem.headline: French markets defensive as election looms.

text.p: French financial markets went on the defensive on Tuesday after the announcement of a snap parliamentary election, and traders said opinion polls would hold the key to moves in the coming days.

Any sign that the opposition Socialists were gaining ground would hit prices, they said. Socialist leader Lionel Jospin has said he opposes further tough fiscal policies to ensure France that meets budget deficit targets for joining European economic and monetary union (EMU).
"We'll be eating, drinking and sleeping polls over the next few weeks," a bond analyst at a French bank said.
President Jacques Chirac called the two-round elections for May 25 and June 1 on Monday evening.

The bond and stock markets stumbled on Tuesday after a shortlived recovery. Traders said the mood was nervous and few investors were willing to stick their necks out by buying until the political horizon became clearer.

"There's a chance the Socialists could come to power and that scares people," an equity trader said. A government announcement on Tuesday that partial privatisation of France Telecom would be delayed by a month because of the vote also weighed on prices.
The CAC-40 index of French blue-chip shares was down 0.85 percent at 2,501.38 points by mid-afternoon. Earlier, it had been down more than one percent.
While markets fear the Socialists would not impose further austerity, equity investors ironically worried that the ruling centre-right coalition would do precisely that if it regained power.

By going early to the polls, the coalition is seeking a mandate for more austerity measures to allow France to meet the three percent budget deficit target for EMU. This could hurt already lacklustre consumption.
The June bond future climbed more than a quarter of point before election jitters knocked it down to trade marginally lower on the day at 128.24.
"The French love an (opinion) poll," a futures trader at a French bank said. "There's going to be a piece of news that will knock this market back."

The early rise in the futures market helped French 10-year bonds to outperform their German counterparts. But later the spread steadied, with French bonds yielding seven basis points less than their German counterparts.
The French franc was trading little changed at 3.3747 against the mark, up from 3.3762 late on Monday just before official confirmation of a snap election.

French interest rate futures, which have come under attack during the past few days, staged a brief rebound but failed to hold their gains. Analysts said the sell-off looked overdone from a fundamental point of view.

The short end of the French yield curve could well offer considerable value as the election neared, they said. There was little likelihood that the Bank of France, flush with mark reserves, would raise official rates to defend the franc.

However, they said the volatility of PIBOR (Paris Interbank Offered Rates) interest rate futures contracts, often subject to large speculative flows from U.S. funds, meant it was not a place for the cautious at the moment.

"The safest part is long end. It's less susceptible to daily volatility," Joanne Perez, strategist at Merrill Lynch in Paris said. "I also don't think investors would be any safer in any other European yield curves, other than Germany, as the risk is that any policy change would go against early EMU."

Iain Lindsay, senior bond analyst at Credit Lyonnais, said: "The safest part of the curve is the long end, the front end is the most vulnerable given the whipsaws PIBOR can have. You just have to go to the long end and sit it out."

"For pure elimination of capital risk you clearly go into cash but it ultimately depends on your benchmark. If you're measured on absolute risk you're better off not being in France at all," Lindsay said.
Analysts also said the long end was relatively well protected as most bonds were held by domestic investors, many of whom had restrictions on their ability to buy overseas assets.
